items.html:
Japan consists of three main terms used to identify land, groupings and borders: Islands, Regions and Prefectures.

  • Islands: The four main islands that make up the country of Japan. From the top they are: Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu.
  • Regions: Some islands are further broken down into groupings of prefectures.
  • Prefectures: These form the currently 47 different subdivisions within the country.

Many of these names are used in this guide, on maps, and when referring to areas of Japan. Therefore, it is recommended to learn and become comfortable with each category, and the titles within.

The appearance of the standard Japanese Google car is often black and white. You may find it in black or rarely with an antenna.

In addition, due to privacy reasons, the camera is intentionally set lower to the ground. This is known as low-cam. You can identify it by:

  • Looking downwards. The blur will be noticeably larger.
  • The road will look wider, and objects will be viewed from a lower perspective.

NOTE: The only other country that always has low-cam is Switzerland. It can also be seen in Generation 4 coverage in Sri Lanka. Also, the car will be blurred in Switzerland.

Japan drives on the left hand side of the road.

NOTE: Hong Kong drives on the left hand side of the road, same as Japan. South Korea and Taiwan drive on the right hand side instead.

Japanese is written with a mixture of three main systems: kanji and two syllabic scripts: hiragana and katakana. Formal signs and texts will mostly use kanji and hiragana. The kanji system is directly borrowed from Chinese and thus looks very similar, while the syllabic scripts are more loosely inspired by Chinese. Hiragana generally looks simpler than Chinese characters, many of the symbols have loops, which are not present in Chinese. The shapes are also typically slightly softer than the shapes present in most kanji.

_You can learn more about hiragana, katakana and kanji in the region guessing section, learning frequent terms and names._

Katakana is mainly used for loan words, and are thus common to find in commercials. They are generally quite simple, with a lot of geometrical shapes rather than the more artistic shapes present in hiragana and kanji.

On the left hand side you can find the pronunciation and meaning of eight of the most commonly featured kanji in town and city names. Learning to recognise these can make finding cities considerably easier.

On the right you see the shape and pronunciation of the cardinal directions and the shape of some kanji commonly found at the end of place names. If you see the kanji for prefecture or city, chances are you will be able to find it fairly quickly. Wards are typically findable granted you know the city, while towns are often fairly difficult to locate.

NOTE: Most of these kanji have alternative, less common pronunciations.

Japanese architecture has many distinct and expressive styles, with many unique buildings. These can range from traditional country houses, regional designs, modern large cities, coastal reinforced buildings, and anything in between.

_You can learn more about different types of architecture and styles in the region guessing section._

Japan mostly uses these round concrete poles, which have these screw-like extensions. Other information can often be found on or attached to the pole including:

  • Electrical plates.
  • Guy-wires.
  • Pole reflectors.

Therefore, they are a key asset in region guessing Japan.

_You can learn more about plates, reflectors, and guy-wires in the region guessing section._

You can find a variety of pole reflectors in Japan. They are typically short and do not touch the ground. Common patterns found all across Japan include:

  • Yellow vertical stripes.
  • Yellow diagonal stripes.
  • Vertical or diagonal white stripes.

NOTE: The Taiwanese variant has diagonal stripes that reach the ground. The South Korean ones have diagonal, thicker stripes.

_You can learn more about the different regional reflectors in the region guessing section._
Japan uses a standard short white licence plate with green text. You will often see a different short yellow version with black text issued to “light automobiles”, otherwise known as Kei Cars.

Japan has three common variations of road lines. They are as follows:

  • The most common being white, solid outer lines with a dashed white middle line.
  • White solid sidelines with a yellow solid middle line.
  • White solid sidelines with yellow and white middle lines.

While you may find other, more rare combinations, Japan will never have yellow outside road lines.

Japan usually uses simple white bollards with circular reflector(s) on the top. However, sometimes these bollards are black, or have other extensions. They can also have the city or prefecture written on it in kanji.

_You can learn more about the bollards and kanji in the region guessing section._

Japan generally uses these simple, white guardrails.

_You can learn more about the exceptions in the region guessing section._

Prefecture roads are identified by their hexagonal-shaped shields. The prefecture is often written under the road number in kanji. While the shield design remains, other variations can be found:

  • On prefectural highway shields (with kanji).
  • On directional intersection signs.
  • Or on small, directional arrow signs.

As multiple prefectures can have the same road number, it is recommended to first find the prefecture you are in.

Some frequently seen infrastructure in Japan consists of:

  • This unique stop sign.
  • A school pedestrian crossing.
  • And these traffic mirrors.

While many infrastructural clues exist, these three are very common, and may very well help you identify Japan on a difficult round.
Retaining walls can be an excellent clue for Japan in rural areas with little to no information.

Area codes are commonly found throughout the country and increase to the south.

NOTE: Area codes ending with a 0 are often not regional, most notably 0120.
Every region in Japan features a distinct plate on their utility poles.
The pole reflector pads vary by region in Japan. But generic designs can be found nationwide.
You can narrow down the prefecture you are in based on the style of road diamond.
Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

Most regions in Japan have unique guy wires.

NOTE: Only the most consistent ones are on this map.
You may sometimes find an orange arrow located above the top most pole plate in Chugoku.
These orange and black bands wrapped around poles can often be found in Shikoku.

These attachments with an approximately 120-degree angle can commonly be found on poles in Kansai.

NOTE: Sometimes there is no angle, and instead just an angled downward attachment.
These smaller attachments with a 90-degree angle can commonly be found on poles in Shikoku.

The electrical poles in Hokkaido either have this plus-shaped bar attached to the side of the pole, or one transformer mounted on two bars.

However, if there is more than one transformer, they will often be mounted on the sides of a square.

NOTE: While the Kanto transformer may also be mounted on two bars, Hokkaido will never have a wooden plate.

The transformers in Tohoku, which often have additional square holding brackets and the logo of the Tohoku Electrical Company, are sometimes mounted on a round plate with a zigzag bar.

Furthermore, you may also find transformers mounted on the side of a square, with a straight bar mounted on the top of the square. Rarely, you may find a square without a bar.

NOTE: While Kansai may have a square attachment as well, the bar will be mounted on the bottom rather than the top.

The transformers in Kanto, which can have three or two insulators, are often mounted on a wooden plate and two bars, or a round plate and a T-shaped bar.

NOTE: While the Hokkaido transformer may also be mounted on two bars, it will never have a wooden plate. Kanto ones can also be mounted without a wooden plate.

The transformers in Hokuriku, which are attached with thin metal bars, often have these small “lamp” shaped insulators. There will never be a bar present except for the attachment mentioned above.

NOTE: The prefecture of Niigata will have the Tohoku transformer design, as opposed to Hokuriku one.
The transformers in Chubu, which often have painted yellow numbers and black “tap” connectors, are either attached with large triangle and horizontal bars, or these thin metal brackets.

The transformers in Kansai have either a straight or zigzag bar mounted on the bottom of a square. The transformer(s) will be mounted on the sides of that same square.

While this is uncommon, the bar and transformer(s) may be mounted on a vertical bar, rather than a square.

NOTE: While Tohoku may have a square attachment as well, the bar will be mounted on the top rather than the bottom.

The transformers in Chugoku, which have a cross-shaped bar attached in the middle of the pole, mounted by a full triangle, will have a long horizontal or short vertical insulator(s) at the end.

A white sticker will often be stuck to the bottom of the transformer with red numbers. They may also be painted on the side.

The transformers in Shikoku, which also have a cross-shaped bar attached in the middle of the pole, mounted by a half triangle, will have “hat shaped” short horizontal insulators at the end.

A white sticker will often be stuck to the bottom of the transformer with black numbers.
The transformers in Kyushu, which have a straight bar attached on the side of the pole with three insulators at the end, will have transformers mounted 180-degrees from one another.
Transformers in Okinawa, which have a T-shaped bar attached on the side of the pole, will have transformers mounted on opposite sides of the pole.
These grey “insulator-esque” blocks, which wires are fed through, can be found in the regions of Chubu, Kansai, Chugoku, Shikoku, and very rarely in Hokkaido.
This pole top, with four thicker bars and a circle piece at the top, is common in the Chubu region.
This pole top, with two sides filled in and shaped like a tent, is common in the Hokuriku region.
This pole top, with four thin, skinny bars, is common in the Chugoku region.
This tuning fork pole top, with a long top bar that sticks out each end and horizontal bar(s) below, is found the majority of the time in the Kanto region.
This tuning fork pole top, with a short top bar and horizontal bar below, is found the majority of the time in the Chubu region.
This tuning fork pole top, with a thin wire and horizontal bar below, is common in the Kansai region.

This infrastructural arrow informs drivers of where the shoulder line is when under snow, and is located almost exclusively in Hokkaido.

NOTE: While much more rare, other variations can be found here:

  • This arrow, found in the Aomori prefecture (or more rarely Hokkaido), has distinct silver bolts around the border.
  • This variation, found in the Gifu prefecture, is long and thin.
  • This alternate yellow and black design can often be found on the northern part of National Highway 275 in Hokkaido.
  • This yellow and green arrow is found southwest of Sapporo.
  • This yellow and black arrow can be found on Hokkaido.

This flat, white bollard, found on the island of Kyushu and in Yamaguchi Prefecture, will have a series of separated orange reflectors on one side, and the same white on the opposite.

NOTE: Rarely, you may find similar bollards in Hokkaido. However, both sides will have orange reflectors.
Some bollards on the island of Shikoku can have a black stripe just under the reflector. They can be found normally, attached to guardrails or walls.

This thick, white bollard, found in the Tohoku region, will have an octagonal reflector, and yellow stripe just underneath. In addition, you can find the same bollard, but with a rectangular top.

Finally, there are two other variations. You can find a black octagonal, and rectangular version. They are often found on National Highways or Expressways and can have the number printed on them.
This bollard, much like Tohoku, will be a thick, white bollard with an octagonal reflector. However, this Akita prefecture variation will have two yellow stripes underneath the reflector.

The Toyama prefecture bollard has one reflector, is extendable and has a red stripe underneath the reflector.

NOTE: Be careful: if there is either a second reflector, or a yellow stripe instead of a red one, these are different bollards. These are more common variations found across many prefectures.
This bollard, with an octagonal reflector, and red stripe underneath it, is exclusive to the Okayama prefecture. Additionally, there will be a sloped connection where the base meets the reflector.
This bollard, found in the Aomori prefecture, has two yellow stripes, a single circular reflector, and is extendable. Sometimes, only one thicker stripe near the top may be present.
These striped bollards (which cover over the original) have a thinner top half, and no reflectors, and are common to the Tohoku region. They are especially common in Akita prefecture.
In the northern parts of the Chugoku region, you can primarily find these basic snow poles, with either a thin extended, or thin contracted top. They can also sometimes be found in Iwate.
Green bands on guardrails are most commonly found in Oita and Miyazaki, but can be found on all of Kyushu.
These distinctive yellow guardrails can be found in the Yamaguchi Prefecture.

You can find these chevron-like stickers, or more rarely orange ones, on guardrails in Hokkaido.

  • On the end or side of a guardrail.
  • Stuck to metal posts between wire fences, which are often found in Hokkaido.
  • On railings, which are often found on bridges, underneath the inside of the railing.
Guardrail endings with these red and yellow striped stickers can commonly be found across Chugoku, except in Yamaguchi. They can also rarely be found in Niigata.
Vertical traffic lights can be found in Hokkaido, and along the northwestern coast. The usual horizontal traffic lights can be found everywhere else.
These specific black signs with two yellow circles are found in Kagawa. Other variations can be seen, including them stacked on top of each other, or with an arrow attached above.

Kerosine tanks, otherwise known as “Claymores”, can be found more commonly the further north you go. They are abundant in Hokkaido, but can be found in prefectures south of it, or in high elevation mountainous areas.

Hot water, gas and propane tanks can be found more frequently in northern prefectures or high elevation mountainous areas. Here are a few common variations you can find:

  • The standard hot water tank.
  • Covered propane tanks.
  • Exposed propane tanks.
  • These cylindrical tanks.
  • And finally, these circular tripod tanks.

Moreover, these are even more common in rural towns or villages, where major water or gas lines are unavailable.
Snow prevention roads, known as ‘Shosetsu’, are found mainly in northwest coastal prefectures. They appear as tiny circles in the pavement, and spray warm underground water to clear snow.

Cycling routes in Ehime use an outside white, with an inside blue line. They are more commonly found along the coast but may be found further inland too.

While exceptions do exist, and can be found in other prefectures, they are the extreme minority.
These unique red-tiled roofs are most commonly found in Chugoku, especially in the prefectures of Hiroshima and Shimane.

The further you are north, roofs generally transition from tiled to level or flat sloped in order to compensate for heavy snowfall. Northern houses often have ladders attached to the side, giving roof access to clear snow.

NOTE: In addition to north to south, high-elevation mountainous regions or high snowfall areas often use such roofs, even in more central or southern prefectures.
Okinawa can often be recognised by the white concrete buildings with flat roofs.

Giant butterbur (commonly referred to as cabbage) is abundant in Hokkaido and some northern prefectures. Plants found south of Hokkaido often have smaller leaves. It is often found growing along the roadside.

NOTE: Cabbage is also found on the island of Sakhalin, Russia. However, the Google car will not have low-cam there.

Green tea plants are often grown in hedged rows. You will often see these fans mounted on poles, which serve the purpose of preventing frost from falling on the plants.

The prefectures of Shizuoka (36%) and Kagoshima (34%) make up the majority of the production, with Mie (7%), Miyazaki (4%), and other prefectures (17%) making up the minority.

Rice is mainly produced north of Tokyo. During growth, it resembles straws of grass. And when ready for harvest, brown husks are visible. They are also commonly planted in beds of water.

The regions of Chubu (21%), Kanto (15%), Tohoku (27%), and Hokkaido (7%) make up the majority of production.

Japanese White Birch grows dominantly in the Chubu and Hokkaido regions, and to a lesser extent in Tohoku. Small areas of white birch can be found throughout Japan, so use this information primarily to help assist your region guess.

NOTE: Japanese Beech is another species of tree found in Japan. They, however, have more grey and spotted bark, as opposed to the mostly white Japanese White Birch.

In general, bamboo grows more often in the south, and slowly decreases further north. Population size and areas where it grows can vary, so use this information primarily in helping assist your region guess.

Chinese Silver Grass, referred to as Kyushu grass, is indeed very abundant on the island of Kyushu. However, use this tip with caution, as they can be seen outside of this area.

NOTE: Another notable region they can be found in is the prefectures of Niigata, Yamagata and Akita. Though, combining the rather large quantity found on Kyushu, its normally distinct vegetation, along with other information, there often will be a clear distinction.
Sugarcane is almost exclusively found on the islands in southern Kyushu and Okinawa.

Hokkaido has very limited winter and snow coverage. Unless you are certain, it is often better not to guess this prefecture. Though, if you do find yourself in Hokkaido, these regions are most likely. Other low amounts of miscellaneous coverage is primarily in the southern half of the island.

Japan is notably a very mountainous country. However, there are some regions that are quite flat, being the Nobi and Kanto plains. While at times they can look very similar, determining that it is one or the other can be very helpful.

NOTE: While there are, of course, other flat areas in Japan, these two are the most recognizable.
You can find these ‘Shisa’ guardian lions and house plaques with these specific characters in Okinawa. The colour and shapes of both can vary.
Agricultural fields with red soil are commonly found on several southern islands, most notably on the islands of Miyakojima and Ishigaki in southern Okinawa.

Mount Fuji is the tallest mountain in Japan, with a gradual incline and often snowy summit.

Depending on the elevation, it can be seen from far away. This can create some excellent region guesses, especially if you account for direction and distance.
Tokyo City features a nice manhole design, with a 5 petal flower and many small circles on the outside.
Cyrillic can be found on signs in the cities of Wakkanai and Nemuro, in northern Hokkaido.
These artistically painted poles, made to resemble birch trees, are unique to the city of Date in Hokkaido.

There are a variety of trekkers and tripods, covering a vast amount of locations which span over multiple prefectures and regions.

_Due to the enormous volume of information on this topic, and it being too large to be contained in this guide, we recommend this resource to learn more about the various trekkers._

steps.title: Maps and resources
steps.html:
GeoGuessr’s own official Japan map is not very focused on information that will help you determine the region or prefecture. Plonk It recommends the following maps instead:

  • A Balanced Japan (map link) - Over 100,000 ai generated locations on intersections from all over Japan.

In addition, here are some resources to help you practice Japan:

  • Plonk It Japan (map link) - Play this map to study the step 2 and 3 tips from this guide.
  • Prefectures of Japan (quiz link) - Familiarise yourself with the prefectures of Japan with this quiz.
  • Prefecture kanji quiz (quiz link) - Learn the kanji for each Japanese prefecture

lm.name: Infrastructure - Transformer - 2 or 3 Insulators
lm.note:
The transformers in Kanto, which can have three or two insulators, are often mounted on a wooden plate and two bars, or a round plate and a T-shaped bar.

NOTE: While the Hokkaido transformer may also be mounted on two bars, it will never have a wooden plate. Kanto ones can also be mounted without a wooden plate.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Transformer - Black Tap Connector
lm.note: The transformers in Chubu, which often have painted yellow numbers and black “tap” connectors, are either attached with large triangle and horizontal bars, or these thin metal brackets.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Transformer - Cross (Chugoku Variant)
lm.note: The transformers in Chugoku, which have a cross-shaped bar attached in the middle of the pole, mounted by a full triangle, will have a long horizontal or short vertical insulator(s) at the end.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Transformer - Cross (Hat Insulator)
lm.note: The transformers in Shikoku, which also have a cross-shaped bar attached in the middle of the pole, mounted by a half triangle, will have “hat shaped” short horizontal insulators at the end.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Transformer - Insulator Box
lm.note: These grey “insulator-esque” blocks, which wires are fed through, can be found in the regions of Chubu, Kansai, Chugoku, Shikoku, and very rarely in Hokkaido.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Transformer - Kyushu
lm.note: The transformers in Kyushu, which have a straight bar attached on the side of the pole with three insulators at the end, will have transformers mounted 180-degrees from one another.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Transformer - Lamp-Shaped Insulator
lm.note:
The transformers in Hokuriku, which are attached with thin metal bars, often have these small “lamp” shaped insulators. There will never be a bar present except for the attachment mentioned above.

NOTE: The prefecture of Niigata will have the Tohoku transformer design, as opposed to Hokuriku one.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Transformer - Metal Bracket
lm.note: The transformers in Chubu, which often have painted yellow numbers and black “tap” connectors, are either attached with large triangle and horizontal bars, or these thin metal brackets.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Transformer - Okinawa
lm.note: Transformers in Okinawa, which have a T-shaped bar attached on the side of the pole, will have transformers mounted on opposite sides of the pole.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Transformer - One on Square
lm.note:
In Tohoku, you may also find transformers mounted on the side of a square, with a straight bar mounted on the top of the square. Rarely, you may find a square without a bar.

NOTE: While Kansai may have a square attachment as well, the bar will be mounted on the bottom rather than the top.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Transformer - Plus-Shaped Bar
lm.note: The electrical poles in Hokkaido either have this plus-shaped bar attached to the side of the pole, or one transformer mounted on two bars.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Transformer - Red Number
lm.note: In Chugoku, a white sticker will often be stuck to the bottom of the transformer with red numbers. They may also be painted on the side.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Transformer - Round Plate / T-Bar
lm.note:
The transformers in Kanto, which can have three or two insulators, are often mounted on a wooden plate and two bars, or a round plate and a T-shaped bar.

NOTE: While the Hokkaido transformer may also be mounted on two bars, it will never have a wooden plate. Kanto ones can also be mounted without a wooden plate.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Transformer - Round Plate / Zigzag Bar
lm.note: The transformers in Tohoku, which often have additional square holding brackets and the logo of the Tohoku Electrical Company, are sometimes mounted on a round plate with a zigzag bar.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Transformer - Square / Bottom Bar
lm.note:
The transformers in Kansai have either a straight or zigzag bar mounted on the bottom of a square. The transformer(s) will be mounted on the sides of that same square.

While this is uncommon, the bar and transformer(s) may be mounted on a vertical bar, rather than a square.

NOTE: While Tohoku may have a square attachment as well, the bar will be mounted on the top rather than the bottom

lm.name: Infrastructure - Transformer - Triangle
lm.note: The transformers in Chubu, which often have painted yellow numbers and black “tap” connectors, are either attached with large triangle and horizontal bars, or these thin metal brackets.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Transformer - Two Bars
lm.note: The electrical poles in Hokkaido either have this plus-shaped bar attached to the side of the pole, or one transformer mounted on two bars. The Kanto Transformer may also be mounted on two bars.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Transformer - Two on Square
lm.note: In Hokkaido, if there is more than one transformer, they will often be mounted on the sides of a square.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Transformer - White Sticker
lm.note: A white sticker will often be stuck to the bottom of the transformer with black numbers.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Transformer - Wooden Plate
lm.note:

lm.name: Infrastructure - Tuning Fork - Chubu
lm.note: This tuning fork pole top, with a short top bar and horizontal bar below, is found the majority of the time in the Chubu region.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Tuning Fork - Kansai

lm.name: Infrastructure - Tuning Fork - Kanto

lm.name: Infrastructure - Vertical Traffic Light
lm.note: Vertical traffic lights can be found in Hokkaido, and along the northwestern coast. The usual horizontal traffic lights can be found everywhere else.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Yellow Circle Sign
lm.note: These specific black signs with two yellow circles are found in Kagawa. Other variations can be seen, including them stacked on top of each other, or with an arrow attached above.

lm.name: Landscape - Mount Fuji
lm.note:
Mount Fuji is the tallest mountain in Japan, with a gradual incline and often snowy summit.

Depending on the elevation, it can be seen from far away. This can create some excellent region guesses, especially if you account for direction and distance.

lm.name: Landscape - Plains
lm.note:
Japan is notably a very mountainous country. However, there are some regions that are quite flat, being the Nobi and Kanto plains. While at times they can look very similar, determining that it is one or the other can be very helpful.

NOTE: While there are, of course, other flat areas in Japan, these two are the most recognizable.

lm.name: Language - Cyrillic
lm.note: Cyrillic can be found on signs in the cities of Wakkanai and Nemuro, in northern Hokkaido.

lm.name: Vegetation - Bamboo
lm.note: In general, bamboo grows more often in the south, and slowly decreases further north. Population size and areas where it grows can vary, so use this information primarily in helping assist your region guess.

lm.name: Vegetation - Chinese Silver Grass
lm.note:
Chinese Silver Grass, referred to as Kyushu grass, is indeed very abundant on the island of Kyushu. However, use this tip with caution, as they can be seen outside of this area.

NOTE: Another notable region they can be found in is the prefectures of Niigata, Yamagata and Akita. Though, combining the rather large quantity found on Kyushu, its normally distinct vegetation, along with other information, there often will be a clear distinction.

lm.name: Vegetation - Giant Butterbur
lm.note: Giant butterbur (commonly referred to as cabbage) is abundant in Hokkaido and some northern prefectures. Plants found south of Hokkaido often have smaller leaves. It is often found growing along the roadside.

lm.name: Vegetation - Japanese White Birch
lm.note:
Japanese White Birch grows dominantly in the Chubu and Hokkaido regions, and to a lesser extent in Tohoku. Small areas of white birch can be found throughout Japan, so use this information primarily to help assist your region guess.

NOTE: Japanese Beech is another species of tree found in Japan. They, however, have more grey and spotted bark, as opposed to the mostly white Japanese White Birch.

lm.name: Kansai Transformer

While this is uncommon, the bar and transformer(s) may be mounted on a vertical bar, rather than a square.

NOTE: While Tohoku may have a square attachment as well, the bar will be mounted on the top rather than the bottom.

lm.name: Kanto Transformer
lm.note:

lm.name: Kyushu Transformer
lm.note: The transformers in Kyushu, which have a straight bar attached on the side of the pole with three insulators at the end, will have transformers mounted 180-degrees from one another.

lm.name: Okinawa Transformer

lm.name: Shikoku Transformer
lm.note:

A white sticker will often be stuck to the bottom of the transformer with black numbers.

lm.name: Tohoku Transformer
lm.note:
The transformers in Tohoku, which often have additional square holding brackets and the logo of the Tohoku Electrical Company, are sometimes mounted on a round plate with a zigzag bar.

Furthermore, you may also find transformers mounted on the side of a square, with a straight bar mounted on the top of the square. Rarely, you may find a square without a bar.

NOTE: While Kansai may have a square attachment as well, the bar will be mounted on the bottom rather than the top.

  • The blur will be noticeably larger.
  • The road will look wider, and objects will be viewed from a lower perspective.

lm.note: This bollard, found in the Aomori prefecture, has two yellow stripes, a single circular reflector, and is extendable. Sometimes, only one thicker stripe near the top may be present.

lm.name: Bollards
lm.note: In Japan, simple white bollards with circular or rectangular reflectors at the top are commonly used. However, sometimes these bollards are black, or have other extensions. They can also have the city or prefecture written on it in kanji.

lm.name: Kyushu/Yamaguchi Bollard
lm.note:
This flat, white bollard, found on the island of Kyushu and in Yamaguchi Prefecture, will have a series of separated orange reflectors on one side, and the same white on the opposite.

NOTE: Rarely, you may find similar bollards in Hokkaido. However, both sides will have orange reflectors.

lm.name: Okayama Bollard
lm.note: This bollard, with an octagonal reflector, and red stripe underneath it, is exclusive to the Okayama prefecture. Additionally, there will be a sloped connection where the base meets the reflector.

lm.name: Striped Bollard
lm.note: These striped bollards (which cover over the original) have a thinner top half, and no reflectors, and are common to the Tohoku region. They are especially common in Akita prefecture.

lm.name: Tohoku Bollard
lm.note:
This thick, white bollard, found in the Tohoku region, will have an octagonal reflector, and yellow stripe just underneath. In addition, you can find the same bollard, but with a rectangular top.

Finally, there are two other variations. You can find a black octagonal, and rectangular version. They are often found on National Highways or Expressways and can have the number printed on them.

lm.name: Toyama Bollard
lm.note:
The Toyama prefecture bollard has one reflector, is extendable and has a red stripe underneath the reflector.

NOTE: Be careful: if there is either a second reflector, or a yellow stripe instead of a red one, these are different bollards. These are more common variations found across many prefectures.

lm.note:

  • Northern houses often have ladders attached to the side, giving roof access to clear snow.

--- NOTE:

lm.name: Green Tea
lm.note:
Green tea plants are often grown in hedged rows. You will often see these fans mounted on poles, which serve the purpose of preventing frost from falling on the plants.

The prefectures of Shizuoka (36%) and Kagoshima (34%) make up the majority of the production, with Mie (7%), Miyazaki (4%), and other prefectures (17%) making up the minority.

lm.name: Grey "Insulator-Esque" Blocks
lm.note: These grey “insulator-esque” blocks, which wires are fed through, can be found in the regions of Chubu, Kansai, Chugoku, Shikoku, and very rarely in Hokkaido.

lm.name: Hokkaido Pole
lm.note:
The electrical poles in Hokkaido either have this plus-shaped bar attached to the side of the pole, or one transformer mounted on two bars.

However, if there is more than one transformer, they will often be mounted on the sides of a square.

NOTE: While the Kanto transformer may also be mounted on two bars, Hokkaido will never have a wooden plate.

lm.name: Hokkaido Pole Plate
lm.note:
Every region in Japan features a distinct plate on their utility poles.

The Hokkaido pole plate is the plate with the highest amount of characters on one plate.

lm.name: Hokkaido Signpost Sticker
lm.note: Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

lm.name: Hokuriku Pole
lm.note:
The transformers in Hokuriku, which are attached with thin metal bars, often have these small “lamp” shaped insulators. There will never be a bar present except for the attachment mentioned above.

NOTE: The prefecture of Niigata will have the Tohoku transformer design, as opposed to Hokuriku one.

lm.name: Hokuriku Pole Plate
lm.note:
Every region in Japan features a distinct plate on their utility poles.

There are multiple horizontal plates attached to the poles in Hokuriku. They are including NTT

lm.name: Hokuriku Pole Reflector
lm.note: The pole reflector pads vary by region in Japan.

lm.name: Hokuriku Pole Top
lm.note: This pole top, with two sides filled in and shaped like a tent, is common in the Hokuriku region.

lm.name: Hyogo Signpost Sticker
lm.note: Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

lm.name: Ibaraki Signpost Sticker
lm.note: Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

lm.name: Infrastructural Arrow (Highway 275)
lm.note:
This infrastructural arrow informs drivers of where the shoulder line is when under snow, and is located almost exclusively in Hokkaido.

This alternate yellow and black design can often be found on the northern part of National Highway 275 in Hokkaido.

lm.name: Infrastructural Arrow (Long)
lm.note:
This infrastructural arrow informs drivers of where the shoulder line is when under snow, and is located almost exclusively in Hokkaido.

This variation, found in the Gifu prefecture, is long and thin.

lm.name: Infrastructural Arrow (normal)
lm.note: This infrastructural arrow informs drivers of where the shoulder line is when under snow, and is located almost exclusively in Hokkaido.

lm.name: Infrastructural Arrow (Silver Bolts)
lm.note:
This infrastructural arrow informs drivers of where the shoulder line is when under snow, and is located almost exclusively in Hokkaido.

This arrow, found in the Aomori prefecture (or more rarely Hokkaido), has distinct silver bolts around the border.

lm.name: Infrastructural Arrow (Yellow/Black)
lm.note:
This infrastructural arrow informs drivers of where the shoulder line is when under snow, and is located almost exclusively in Hokkaido.

This yellow and black arrow can be found on Hokkaido.

lm.name: Infrastructural Arrow (Yellow/Green)
lm.note:
This infrastructural arrow informs drivers of where the shoulder line is when under snow, and is located almost exclusively in Hokkaido.

This yellow and green arrow is found southwest of Sapporo.

lm.name: Japanese White Birch
lm.note:
Japanese White Birch grows dominantly in the Chubu and Hokkaido regions, and to a lesser extent in Tohoku. Small areas of white birch can be found throughout Japan, so use this information primarily to help assist your region guess.

NOTE: Japanese Beech is another species of tree found in Japan. They, however, have more grey and spotted bark, as opposed to the mostly white Japanese White Birch.

lm.name: Kagawa Road Diamond
lm.note: You can narrow down the prefecture you are in based on the style of road diamond.

lm.name: Kagawa Sign
lm.note: These specific black signs with two yellow circles are found in Kagawa. Other variations can be seen, including them stacked on top of each other, or with an arrow attached above.

lm.name: Kanagawa Signpost Sticker
lm.note: Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

lm.name: Kansai Pole
lm.note:
The transformers in Kansai have either a straight or zigzag bar mounted on the bottom of a square. The transformer(s) will be mounted on the sides of that same square.

While this is uncommon, the bar and transformer(s) may be mounted on a vertical bar, rather than a square.

NOTE: While Tohoku may have a square attachment as well, the bar will be mounted on the top rather than the bottom.

lm.name: Kansai Pole Plate
lm.note:
Every region in Japan features a distinct plate on their utility poles.

This plate can be recognized by the Japanese written vertically in the middle/ on the right with other characters written in rows of two. In the bottom left and right corner are also other characters written.

lm.name: Kansai Pole Reflector
lm.note: The pole reflector pads vary by region in Japan.

lm.name: Kansai Pole Top
lm.note: This tuning fork pole top, with a thin wire and horizontal bar below, is common in the Kansai region.

lm.name: Kansai/Hokuriku/Shikoku Guy Wire
lm.note:
Most regions in Japan have unique guy wires.

NOTE: Only the most consistent ones are on this map.

lm.name: Kanto Pole
lm.note:
The transformers in Kanto, which can have three or two insulators, are often mounted on a wooden plate and two bars, or a round plate and a T-shaped bar.

NOTE: While the Hokkaido transformer may also be mounted on two bars, Tokyo will always have a wooden plate.

lm.name: Kanto Pole Plate
lm.note: Every region in Japan features a distinct plate on their utility poles.

lm.name: Kanto Pole Top
lm.note: This tuning fork pole top, with a long top bar that sticks out each end and horizontal bar(s) below, is found the majority of the time in the Kanto region.

lm.name: Kumamoto Signpost Sticker
lm.note:
Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

These sticker in the prefecture of Kumamoto can also be found in Kagoshima and Miyazaki (In Kagoshima and Miyazaki, they can have changed colors)

lm.name: Kyushu Pole
lm.note: The transformers in Kyushu, which have a straight bar attached on the side of the pole with three insulators at the end, will have transformers mounted 180-degrees from one another.

lm.name: Kyushu Pole Platew
lm.note:
Every region in Japan features a distinct plate on their utility poles.

The Kyushu plate has a small logo on top, under the logo there are 3 numbers written horizontally and then 4 characters written vertically on the right.

lm.name: Kyushu/Okinawa Guy Wire
lm.note:
Most regions in Japan have unique guy wires.

NOTE: Only the most consistent ones are on this map.

lm.name: Kyushu/Okinawa Pole Reflector
lm.note: The pole reflector pads vary by region in Japan.

lm.name: Kyushu/Yamaguchi Bollard
lm.note:
This flat, white bollard, found on the island of Kyushu and in Yamaguchi Prefecture, will have a series of separated orange reflectors on one side, and the same white on the opposite.

NOTE: Rarely, you may find similar bollards in Hokkaido. However, both sides will have orange reflectors.

lm.name: Manhole Design
lm.note: Tokyo City features a nice manhole design, with a 5 petal flower and many small circles on the outside.

lm.name: Mie Road Diamond
lm.note:
You can narrow down the prefecture you are in based on the style of road diamond.

This road diamond can also be found in the Kochi prefecture. In the Kumamoto and Ishikawa prefecture it is the same design, but in a thinner version.

lm.name: Miyagi Road Diamond
lm.note:
You can narrow down the prefecture you are in based on the style of road diamond.

This road diamond can also be found in the Kyoto, Hyogo and Okayama prefecture. In the Tokushima and Hiroshima prefecture it is the same design, but in a smaller version.

lm.name: Miyagi Signpost Sticker
lm.note: Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

lm.name: Nagano Signpost Sticker
lm.note: Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

lm.name: Nagasaki Signpost Sticker
lm.note:
Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

This design can also be found in the Saga prefectur.

lm.name: Nara Signpost Sticker
lm.note: Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

lm.name: Northern House
lm.note:
The further you are north, roofs generally transition from tiled to level or flat sloped in order to compensate for heavy snowfall. Northern houses often have ladders attached to the side, giving roof access to clear snow.

NOTE: In addition to north to south, high-elevation mountainous regions or high snowfall areas often use such roofs, even in more central or southern prefectures.

lm.name: Oita Signpost Sticker
lm.note: Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

lm.name: Okayama Bollard
lm.note: This bollard, with an octagonal reflector, and red stripe underneath it, is exclusive to the Okayama prefecture. Additionally, there will be a sloped connection where the base meets the reflector.

lm.name: Okayama Signpost Sticker
lm.note: Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

lm.name: Okinawa House
lm.note: Okinawa can often be recognised by the white concrete buildings with flat roofs.

lm.name: Okinawa Pole
lm.note: Transformers in Okinawa, which have a T-shaped bar attached on the side of the pole, will have transformers mounted on opposite sides of the pole.

lm.name: Okinawa Pole Plate
lm.note: Every region in Japan features a distinct plate on their utility poles.

lm.name: Orange and Black Band
lm.note: These orange and black bands wrapped around poles can often be found in Shikoku.

lm.name: Orange Arrow
lm.note: You may sometimes find an orange arrow located above the top most pole plate in Chugoku.

lm.name: Osaka Signpost Sticker
lm.note: Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

lm.name: Plains
lm.note:
Japan is notably a very mountainous country. However, there are some regions that are quite flat, being the Nobi and Kanto plains. While at times they can look very similar, determining that it is one or the other can be very helpful.

NOTE: While there are, of course, other flat areas in Japan, these two are the most recognizable.

lm.name: Red Field
lm.note: Agricultural fields with red soil are commonly found on several southern islands, most notably on the islands of Miyakojima and Ishigaki in southern Okinawa.

lm.name: Red-Tiled Roof
lm.note: These unique red-tiled roofs are most commonly found in Chugoku, especially in the prefectures of Hiroshima and Shimane.

lm.name: Red/Yellow Sticker
lm.note: Guardrail endings with these red and yellow striped stickers can commonly be found across Chugoku, except in Yamaguchi. They can also rarely be found in Niigata.

lm.name: Rice
lm.note:
Rice is mainly produced north of Tokyo. During growth, it resembles straws of grass. And when ready for harvest, brown husks are visible. They are also commonly planted in beds of water.

The regions of Chubu (21%), Kanto (15%), Tohoku (27%), and Hokkaido (7%) make up the majority of production.

lm.name: Shikoku Bollard
lm.note: Some bollards on the island of Shikoku can have a black stripe just under the reflector. They can be found normally, attached to guardrails or walls.

lm.name: Shikoku Pole
lm.note:
The transformers in Shikoku, which also have a cross-shaped bar attached in the middle of the pole, mounted by a half triangle, will have “hat shaped” short horizontal insulators at the end.

A white sticker will often be stuck to the bottom of the transformer with black numbers.

lm.name: Shikoku Pole Plate
lm.note:
Every region in Japan features a distinct plate on their utility poles.

The Shikoku pole plate can be recognized by the "4-squares"-Logo, that stands for the 4 prefectures on the island of Shikoku and the multiple rows of characters from left to right below.

lm.name: Shikoku Pole Reflector
lm.note: The pole reflector pads vary by region in Japan.

lm.name: Shimane Signpost Sticker
lm.note:
Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

The color of the band can vary in this prefectur.

lm.name: Shisa
lm.note: You can find these ‘Shisa’ guardian lions and house plaques with these specific characters in Okinawa. The colour and shapes of both can vary.

lm.name: Shizuoka Road Diamond
lm.note: You can narrow down the prefecture you are in based on the style of road diamond.

lm.name: Shizuoka Signpost Sticker
lm.note: Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

lm.name: Snow Poles
lm.note: In the northern parts of the Chugoku region, you can primarily find these basic snow poles, with either a thin extended, or thin contracted top. They can also sometimes be found in Iwate.

lm.name: Snow Prevention Road
lm.note: Snow prevention roads, known as ‘Shosetsu’, are found mainly in northwest coastal prefectures. They appear as tiny circles in the pavement, and spray warm underground water to clear snow.

lm.name: Striped Bollard
lm.note: These striped bollards (which cover over the original) have a thinner top half, and no reflectors, and are common to the Tohoku region. They are especially common in Akita prefecture.

lm.name: Sugarcane
lm.note: Sugarcane is almost exclusively found on the islands in southern Kyushu and Okinawa.

lm.name: Tochigi Road Diamond
lm.note:
You can narrow down the prefecture you are in based on the style of road diamond.

This design can also be found in the Ibaraki, Saitama and Niigata prefectur.

lm.name: Tohoku Bollard
lm.note:
This thick, white bollard, found in the Tohoku region, will have an octagonal reflector, and yellow stripe just underneath. In addition, you can find the same bollard, but with a rectangular top.

Finally, there are two other variations. You can find a black octagonal, and rectangular version. They are often found on National Highways or Expressways and can have the number printed on them.

lm.name: Tohoku Pole
lm.note:
The transformers in Tohoku, which often have additional square holding brackets and the logo of the Tohoku Electrical Company, are sometimes mounted on a round plate with a zigzag bar.

Furthermore, you may also find transformers mounted on the side of a square, with a straight bar mounted on the top of the square. Rarely, you may find a square without a bar.

NOTE: While Kansai may have a square attachment as well, the bar will be mounted on the bottom rather than the top.

lm.name: Tohoku Pole Plate
lm.note:
Every region in Japan features a distinct plate on their utility poles.

The Tohoku pole plates can be recognized by the fact, that one plate is vertical and longer and the other plate is silver, short and horizontally.

lm.name: Tohoku Pole Reflectors
lm.note: The pole reflector pads vary by region in Japan.

lm.name: Tokushima Signpost Sticker
lm.note: Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

lm.name: Tokyo Signpost Sticker
lm.note: Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

lm.name: Tottori Road Diamond
lm.note:
You can narrow down the prefecture you are in based on the style of road diamond.

This design can also be found in the Shima and Saga prefectur.

lm.name: Tottori Signpost Sticker
lm.note: Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

lm.name: Toyama Bollard
lm.note:
The Toyama prefecture bollard has one reflector, is extendable and has a red stripe underneath the reflector.

NOTE: Be careful: if there is either a second reflector, or a yellow stripe instead of a red one, these are different bollards. These are more common variations found across many prefectures.

lm.name: Toyama Road Diamond
lm.note:
You can narrow down the prefecture you are in based on the style of road diamond.

This design can also be found in the Oita prefecture.

lm.name: Vertical Traffic Light
lm.note: Vertical traffic lights can be found in Hokkaido, and along the northwestern coast. The usual horizontal traffic lights can be found everywhere else.

lm.name: Wakayama Road Diamond
lm.note:
You can narrow down the prefecture you are in based on the style of road diamond.

This design can also be found in the Nara prefecture.

lm.name: Yamagata Signpost Sticker
lm.note:
Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

This design can only be found in the Yamagata prefecture, but the color and amount of the rings can vary.

lm.name: Yamaguchi Signpost Sticker
lm.note: Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

lm.name: Yellow Guardrail
lm.note: These distinctive yellow guardrails can be found in the Yamaguchi Prefecture.

lm.name: Chugoku - Red Tiled Roofs
lm.note: • These unique red-tiled roofs are most commonly found in Chugoku, especially in the prefectures of Hiroshima and Shimane.

lm.name: General Architecture
lm.note:
• Japanese architecture has many distinct and expressive styles, with many unique buildings.
  • These can range from traditional country houses, regional designs, modern large cities, coastal reinforced buildings, and anything in between.

lm.name: Okinawa - White Buildings & Flat Roofs
lm.note: • Okinawa can often be recognised by the white concrete buildings with flat roofs.

lm.name: Chubu/Okinawa guy-wire
lm.note: Wide black and yellow striped guy-wires are commonly found in Chubu. Be aware that these are also found in Okinawa

lm.name: Chubu/Okinawa guy-wire difference
lm.note: It's relatively easy to distinguish Okinawa from Chubu, and doing so can earn you valuable points. While both regions use the same type of guy-wire, Okinawa uses straight-lined reflectors, in contrast to Chubu's twisted reflectors.

lm.name: Chugoku guy-wire
lm.note: Orange or yellow guy-wires with and obvious bulge close to the ground are found in Chugoku. They can also be found in single-wire versions.

lm.name: Kyushu guy-wire
lm.note: Kyushu-style guy-wires are easy to spot by their “paddle” shape, unlike the “bottle” or “baseball bat” shapes of Southern styles. They sometimes can have two thin wires joining a thick base.

lm.name: Kyushu guy-wire in Okinawa
lm.note: Kyushu guy-wires are also found in Okinawa, which makes them hard to tell apart—especially since both regions use the same reflector pads. Because this can cost or earn you a lot of points in later rounds, I still wanted to give you a way to differentiate them. That’s where this pole plate meta comes in. Fortunately, it’s one of the simplest and most recognizable: it's the only one with horizontal bars between the characters, and it's exclusive to Okinawa. This basically makes the guy-wire meta secondary, but it’s still a useful clue that you might be in Okinawa and should check the pole plate.

lm.name: Northern guy-wire
lm.note: Northern-style guy-wires have a smooth, cylindrical cover with yellow and black stripes. There are two types—thin and thick—and while both appear in the same regions, their distribution may vary slightly. They're mostly found in northern Japan, except for Shikoku, which is an outlier with mixed styles.

lm.name: Shikoku guy-wire
lm.note: Shikoku Guy-Wires are usually either Northern or Wa-To types, but what sets them apart is their pairing with the Shikoku pole reflector pad—a short pad with six clear stripes. This combo is a strong sign you're in Shikoku. Be careful not to mix it up with the similar Kansai reflector, which is longer and often faded in color.

lm.name: Tohoku guy-wire
lm.note: Tohokur Guy-Wires are a unique variant of the Northern style, featuring a distinct bulge near the ground. This shape gives them a mixed appearance, combining elements of both Northern and Chugoku guy-wires. They're only found in the Tohoku region of Japan, where their unusual shape makes them easy to identify despite some similarities to nearby styles. From a distance, they may be confused with Northern guy-wires, but the bulge near the bottom sets them apart up close.

lm.name: Wa-To guy-wires
lm.note: Wa-To guy-wires have a distinctive bottle shape with yellow-black stripes and can be easily distinguished from similar types when viewed up close. They are mainly found in western and central Japan – from Wakayama to Toyama – as well as throughout Shikoku, where they are less common but still present everywhere.

lm.name: 1 to 6 Plates - Okinawa
lm.note: In Okinawa, utility pole plates have numbers from 1 to 6 (except 5) at the top, which can help with region guessing. For example, as you can see in the image, the south of Okinawa is 2, the north is 6, and the Okinawa Islands are 1.

lm.name: 7 Plate - Miyako Islands
lm.note:
• In the Miyako Islands, utility pole plates have the number 7 at the top, while in the Yaeyama Islands they have the number 8.
  • Also, Road 390 runs through both island groups but nowhere else, and the landscape with red soil and sugarcane is almost unique to the Yaeyama and Miyako Islands.

lm.name: 8 Plate - Yaeyama Islands
lm.note:
• In the Yaeyama Islands, utility pole plates have the number 8 at the top, while in the Miyako Islands they have the number 7.
  • Also, Road 390 runs through both island groups but nowhere else, and the landscape with red soil and sugarcane is almost unique to the Yaeyama and Miyako Islands.

lm.name: Apple Guardrail - Aomori
lm.note: You’ll find these Apple guardrails in Aomori, mostly in Aomori City (I’m not even sure if you can find them anywhere else in the prefecture)

lm.name: Aso Caldera - Kyushu
lm.note: Aso Caldera in Kyushu is one of the world’s largest volcanic calderas. Its vast grasslands, steep green slopes, and active volcano make the landscape strikingly different from most of Japan.

lm.name: Blue Cycling Routes - Ehime
lm.note: Cycling routes in Ehime have a continuous outside white line and inside blue line. If either line is broken or dashed, it's probably not an Ehime route. They're mostly along the coast, but can be inland too. Exceptions are rare. There are also many routes like this on nearby islands such as Osaki Shimozima and Toyoshima (which are not part of Ehime).

lm.name: Colorful Rectangle Sticker - Tochigi
lm.note: In Tochigi, you can often spot a small colorful rectangle sticker (green, blue, white, etc.) on the back of road signs. Warning: A similar meta appears in Akita and Nagasaki, you can see the differences in the images. Update: In Fukui, you can also find something similar, so try to identify the region first.

lm.name: Gassho Zukuri Village - Hokuriku
lm.note: These traditional gassho-zukuri villages can be found in Shirakawa-go and Gokayama, along with their surrounding areas. I also spotted some in Yamanashi, around Lake Saiko

lm.name: Green guardrail bands - Kyushu
lm.note: In Kyushu, especially in Miyazaki and Oita, you can find this green ring or sticker-like band on guardrail posts. It's rarely seen in Fukuoka, Saga, or Nagasaki, and appears to be even more uncommon in the other Kyushu prefectures.

lm.name: Green Reflector - Saga
lm.note: "Saga Green Reflector" are commonly seen on poles at major intersections. Warning : A green reflector can commonly be found in Nagano Prefecture, but this one is different. I’ll add it in a future update.

lm.name: Hakone Plate - Kanagawa
lm.note:
You can find this plate in Hakone. There’s also a brown version which should be unique to Hakone, so if you see them together you can pretty safely guess Hakone. I did spot the "threaded" plate once in Yamanashi, but it seems to be extremely rare.

Again, I’m not 100% sure, so if you see it somewhere else please let me know.

lm.name: Heart Shapes Pole - Hokuriku
lm.note: This pole top, which looks like two little hearts from far away, is mostly Hokuriku (~90%). I've seen a couple in Shikoku, but it seems extremely rare. Warning: Chubu pole tops can bait you — takes time to tell them apart from a distance.

lm.name: Kanji - 県 - 市 - 町 - 道
lm.note: These kanji are pretty important — they help you recognize names like 'Yamaguchi Prefecture' (山口県) or 'Okayama City' (岡山市). The kanji for 'city' or 'prefecture' appears at the end of the name. You can search them on the map or learn the kanji to guess faster.

lm.name: Lake Biwa - Shiga
lm.note:
• Lake Biwa is the largest lake in Japan. It’s easy to recognize not only because of its size, but also thanks to the cherry blossoms lining parts of the shore. The area has a vibe you learn to recognize.
  • I also noticed this reflector/sticker on the guardrails, which seems to be unique to Shiga. I’m not completely sure though.

lm.name: Large Square Sticker - Akita
lm.note: In Akita, you can often spot a small colorful square sticker (green, blue, white, etc.) on the back of road signs (often with something written on it) Warning: A similar meta appears in Nagasaki and Tochigi, you can see the differences in the images.

lm.name: Mount Hachimantai - Akita - Iwate
lm.note:
• Mount Hachimantai is recognizable by its mix of dead trees and conifers.

  • Coverage exists in May 2014 / May–June 2024 (with snow still visible in May) and Oct 2023 (when the trees turn yellow, making the area even easier to recognize).

  • Warning : A similar landscape can be found in Mt. Zao (between Yamagata and Miyagi) along Route 12, but the center line is yellow, not dashed white like in Hachimantai.

Let me know if you spot another similar area.

lm.name: Mount Rishiri - Hokkaidō
lm.note: In Hokkaido, on the northern part of the west coast, you can see Mount Rishiri.

lm.name: Multiple Round Stickers - Shizuoka
lm.note: In Shizuoka, you'll find multiple white and yellow round stickers (inspection seals) on almost every sign or signpost. You shouldn't need another clue to guess the prefecture.

lm.name: Orange ID Plate - Hokkaidō
lm.note: This orange/yellow plate or sticker is unique to Hokkaido. It's not a very important meta, but it can still be useful in no move. Don’t confuse it with the white/yellow Chūgoku plate.

lm.name: Perforated Plate Pole Top - Chubu
lm.note: In Chubu (except Yamanashi and Hokuriku), you’ll find this top pole and two others unique to the area. The fork-shaped one looks like those in Kansai and Kanto, but they’re different. (Saw a rare similar one in Akita too.) Important note : Niigata has the Kanto top pole and the 'Akita' one. Niigata is kind of weird and mixes a lot of meta. If you see something mixing a lot of meta, you’re probably in Niigata or sometimes in Nagano.

lm.name: Red - Chugoku
lm.note: These unique red-tiled roofs are most commonly found in Chugoku, especially in the prefectures of Hiroshima and Shimane.

lm.name: Red and White Bollard - Akita
lm.note: These striped bollards (which cover over the original) have a thinner top half, and no reflectors, and are common to the Tohoku region. They are especially common in Akita prefecture.

lm.name: Red And Yellow Striped Stickers  - Chugoku And Niigata
lm.note: Guardrail endings with these red and yellow striped stickers can commonly be found across Chugoku, except in Yamaguchi. They can also rarely be found in Niigata. (if there’s White Birch around, go to Niigata)

lm.name: Small Colorful Square - Nagasaki
lm.note: In Nagasaki, you can often spot a small colorful square sticker (green, blue, white, etc.) on the back of road signs. Warning: A similar meta appears in Akita and Tochigi. The biggest confusion is a Yamagata sticker that looks just like this but is always yellow. (make sure you are in Kyushu)

lm.name: Snail Reflector - Hiroshima
lm.note: In Hiroshima, you can find this yellow and green reflector/sticker with a snail, the letters 'H.P.', and what seems to be a momiji leaf (or maybe something else). You’ll see it at intersections near traffic lights.

lm.name: Stoplight terminal box - Saitama
lm.note: In Saitama, stoplight terminal box typically has a C.

lm.name: Unique Reflector Design - Kagawa
lm.note: These specific black signs with two yellow circles are found in Kagawa. Other variations can be seen, including them stacked on top of each other, or with an arrow attached above.

lm.name: Unique Road - Miyazaki
lm.note: The Nichinan Kaigan Road (Route 220) runs from Miyazaki to Nichinan, known for its ocean views and tall palm trees dividing the lanes, though they aren't present all along the road. Warning: some roads in Okinawa and Awaji Island (especially near Iwaya on Route 28) may look similar.

lm.name: V Sticker - Gunma
lm.note: This 'V' sticker is unique to Gunma Prefecture, you'll find them behind signs.

lm.name: White And Yellow Reflector - Chiba

In Gunma, you’ll see these wooden signs with two yellow bands at the bottom.

lm.name: Yamaguchi yellow guardrail

lm.name: Chubu Plate

lm.name: Chubu triangle mount

lm.name: Chugoku arrow

lm.name: Chugoku cross-shaped bar

lm.name: Chugoku plate
lm.note: Chugoku plates will have usually written Energia in latin and sometimes they will include logo.

lm.name: Chugoku pole top
lm.note: This pole top is unique to Chugoku, there is similar version that are more thicc so make sure the pole top is thin like the one on the image.

lm.name: Hokkaido Arrows

lm.name: Hokkaido Plate

lm.name: Hokuriku plates
lm.note: Silver horizontal plates with logo on the top right. NTT plates will be also horizontal(in Tohoku NTT plates are vertical, and only Tohoku plate is horizontal).

lm.name: Kansai 120 stepdown
lm.note: These attachments with an approximately 120-degree angle can commonly be found on poles in Kansai.

lm.name: Kansai plate
lm.note: One of the hardest plate to recognize. Have different designs but will have Japanese written in the middle/or the right and then characters below it in rows of 2 and will usually have 2 numbers at the bottom left/right.

lm.name: Kansai pole top
lm.note: This tuning fork pole top, with a thin wire and horizontal bar below, is common in the Kansai region. Make sure it looks exactly the same with that little thing on the wires in the middle(idk how to call it lol)

lm.name: Kansai reflector
lm.note: Tall reflector with washed colors is exclusive to Kansai region.

lm.name: Kansai transformers
lm.note: The transformers in Kansai have either a straight or zigzag bar mounted on the bottom of a square. The transformer(s) will be mounted on the sides of that same square. (Tohoku transformers are mounted in similar way but the bar will be connected to top of the square)

lm.name: Kanto plate
lm.note: Often silver and handwritten characters. Horizontal characters above three vertical digits.

lm.name: Kanto tall hat insulators
lm.note: Those insulators are unique to Kanto region and are easy to spot. They have black "hat" on top of white insulator.

lm.name: Kyushu bulky insulator
lm.note: Black meteor like looking insulator, from far might be confused with Kanto tall-black hat insulator but Kyushu one appears little more bulkier even from far.

lm.name: Kyushu Plates
lm.note: Distinc logo(sometimes might be missing). Three numbers horizontally near the top, with 4 vertical characters below them on the right(1 kana and 3 numbers).

lm.name: Kyushu transformers
lm.note: Transformers mounted opposite side of the pole with a straight bar mounted on the side of the pole with 3 insulators on one side at the end.(Okinawa has T shaped bar)

lm.name: Kyushu/Okinawa guy wire
lm.note: Guy wires that look like paddle are unique to Kyushu and Okinawa.

lm.name: Kyushu/Okinawa reflector.
lm.note: Protruding bumps, sometimes darker reflector in the middle. Can also be found in Okinawa.

lm.name: Okinawa plates
lm.note: Plate with multiple numbers and lines in between them. Often will have more than 2 plates.

lm.name: Okinawa Transformers
lm.note: Transformers mounted opposite side of the pole with a T shaped bar mounted on the side of the pole.(Kyushu has straight bar). Sometimes only 1 transformer is present.

lm.name: Shikoku cross bar
lm.note: The transformers in Shikoku, which also have a cross-shaped bar attached in the middle of the pole, mounted by a half triangle, will have “hat shaped” short horizontal insulators at the end.

lm.name: Shikoku orange band
lm.note: These orange and black bands wrapped around poles can often be found in Shikoku.

lm.name: Shikoku plate
lm.note: Distinct logo that you can remember since it has 4 dots representing 4 prefectures of Shikoku.

lm.name: Shikoku reflector
lm.note: 6 small reflectors with a little strip "connecting" them in the middle.

top.html:
Japan consists of three main terms used to identify land, groupings and borders: Islands, Regions and Prefectures.

  • Islands: The four main islands that make up the country of Japan. From the top they are: Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu.
  • Regions: Some islands are further broken down into groupings of prefectures.
  • Prefectures: These form the currently 47 different subdivisions within the country.

Many of these names are used in this guide, on maps, and when referring to areas of Japan. Therefore, it is recommended to learn and become comfortable with each category, and the titles within.

The appearance of the standard Japanese Google car is often black and white. You may find it in black or rarely with an antenna.

In addition, due to privacy reasons, the camera is intentionally set lower to the ground. This is known as low-cam. You can identify it by:

  • Looking downwards. The blur will be noticeably larger.
  • The road will look wider, and objects will be viewed from a lower perspective.

NOTE: The only other country that always has low-cam is Switzerland. It can also be seen in Generation 4 coverage in Sri Lanka. Also, the car will be blurred in Switzerland.

top.html:
Japanese is written with a mixture of three main systems: kanji and two syllabic scripts: hiragana and katakana. Formal signs and texts will mostly use kanji and hiragana. The kanji system is directly borrowed from Chinese and thus looks very similar, while the syllabic scripts are more loosely inspired by Chinese. Hiragana generally looks simpler than Chinese characters, many of the symbols have loops, which are not present in Chinese. The shapes are also typically slightly softer than the shapes present in most kanji.

_You can learn more about hiragana, katakana and kanji in the region guessing section, learning frequent terms and names._
